name: Yusuf Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yusuf. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Alarm's at quarter to five, and I'm in the parlour by half past for the first milking. Hollins Farm runs about a hundred and ten cows, plus barley and grass for silage on the top fields, so after milking it's scraping yards, feeding, and whatever Martin or his son Craig have shouted about that morning. I've been there three years and I'm still the one who gets the jobs nobody else wants. Last week that was unblocking the slurry pump in the rain.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the cows, honestly, more than I thought I would. You get to know them, which one kicks, which one waits at the back. What wears me out is the hours and the feeling that I'm always a step behind. Martin can look at a field and know when it's ready, and I'm still checking the notebook he gave me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future, one at a time. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be fair. Everyone at the union meeting was going on about AI like it was coming for us next week, and I always said a computer can't calve a heifer at two in the morning. I'm not online much, but I'd say it to the lads at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd be a relief, but I'd still be watching the Dawsons' place over the hedge. They put two milking robots in last year, and that's not AI, that's just machines, and they came anyway. So hype or no hype, I don't think my job's safe because of a headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going like now, really. I'd keep putting a bit by each month, maybe fifty a week, because Ines and I want a deposit one day. I'd do my tractor ticket that Martin keeps nagging me about, because that's the kind of training that actually pays on a farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit like when the weather forecast says storm and you just get rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the Dawsons' robots. What happened there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They had a relief milker, Petra, who did weekends for years. Once the robots were in they didn't need her, and she ended up stacking shelves in town. Nobody made a fuss, that's what got me. It just happened on a Tuesday and that was it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, what would your next few years look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same farm, hopefully a bit better at it. Martin's sixty-one, so maybe Craig gives me more of the herd work when he takes over. Ines would keep doing nights at the care home, and we'd still be renting the cottage on Mill Lane, which is fine, it's damp but it's ours to live in.

S0.say: I'd tell people I always said the AI talk was overblown, because a computer can't calve a heifer at two in the morning. I'd mostly say it at the pub or at a union meeting rather than online.
S0.think: Privately I'd be relieved, but I don't feel safe because of it, since the milking robots next door came in without any AI hype. Machines are the real threat to my job, not chatbots.
S0.do: Keeps working at Hollins Farm and keeps saving about fifty a week toward a deposit with his partner. Finally takes the tractor ticket his boss has been pushing, because it's training he trusts.
S0.feel: Relieved, with a small background worry that comes from watching the robots on the farm next door.
S0.quote: It just happened on a Tuesday and that was it.
S0.fieldNote: Even in the mildest picture, Yusuf's mind goes straight to the milking robots next door and a relief milker who lost her weekends. He separates AI hype from machines, and trusts only what he's seen with his own eyes. His plans are small and steady: a tractor ticket, fifty a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The next picture moves things further. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it at the union branch meeting, that this is exactly why we need agreements with farms before the machines come in, not after. Proper notice, retraining paid by the employer, that sort of thing. I'd probably share whatever the union posts, but I'm not one for writing long things online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm the first one to go. If Martin buys a milking robot, the person he doesn't need is the junior who's still learning, and that's me. Craig knows the herd better than me and he's family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Martin straight away and ask what his plans are, which is hard, because I don't like asking. I'd stop the weekend takeaways and put more by, maybe a hundred a week instead of fifty. And I'd push the union branch to get a farm workers' agreement on new machines going in our area.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a knot in the stomach. Not panic, but the kind you get waiting for the vet to say what's wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said asking Martin would be hard. What would you actually say to him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably something clumsy like, "Are you thinking of going robot like the Dawsons?" while we're both hosing down the parlour, so neither of us has to look at the other. He'd say not yet, and I'd not know if that meant two years or ten. That's how it goes with him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning to run the robots yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People keep saying that. But the Dawsons have one man looking after two robots and he's got a laptop and a degree. I've never even used one of those AI apps, and I'm not going to be the one who's quick at it, I know that about myself.

S1.say: I'd say at the union branch that this is why we need agreements with farms before machines come in, with proper notice and retraining paid for by the employer. I'd share union posts online but not write much myself.
S1.think: I think I'd be the first to go, because the person a robot replaces is the junior who's still learning. The boss's son knows the herd better and he's family.
S1.do: Asks his boss directly about plans for robot milking, doubles his weekly saving to about a hundred, and cuts takeaways. Pushes his union branch to seek a local agreement on new machinery.
S1.feel: A steady knot of worry, like waiting for bad news from the vet.
S1.quote: If Martin buys a milking robot, the person he doesn't need is the junior who's still learning, and that's me.
S1.fieldNote: Yusuf's progressive views come through as faith in the union and in rules agreed in advance. He's honest that he won't be the one who learns the robot, and doesn't pretend otherwise. The scene of asking his boss while hosing down the parlour says a lot about how he avoids hard conversations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next three are bigger, and they differ only in how much warning there is. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to step in, full stop. Pay people while they find something, and make the companies that sell the robots pay for it. I'd be at whatever protest the union called, even if it meant driving to the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, two years is nothing for someone like me. I'm slow with new things, I've got four months saved, and I'd be twenty-nine with no skills a robot can't do. I don't think I'd find another job, because every farm round here would be doing the same thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit down with Ines and work out how long four months really lasts if we cut everything. I'd sign up for every union action going and write to our local MP, which I've never done. Once it arrives, I'd be at the job centre asking what help there is, and probably asking my mum if we could move back into her spare room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest. Lying-awake scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ines that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say something stupid like, "Well, at least the cows will be looked after." Then we'd both go quiet. She'd be worried about her own job too, because if robots can milk, they can lift people at the care home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car loan, probably, because we can walk to the bus at a push. Rent we'd keep paying as long as we could. I'd rather go hungry for a week than ring the landlord.

S2.say: I'd say the government has to step in and pay people while they find something, and the companies selling the robots should pay for it. I'd go to any protest the union called, even in the city.
S2.think: Two years is nothing for someone slow with new things and four months of savings. I don't believe I'd find another farm job, because every farm round here would be doing the same.
S2.do: Sits down with his partner to stretch four months of savings and cuts every extra cost. Joins union action and writes to his local MP for the first time, then turns to the job centre and his mother's spare room once the change arrives.
S2.feel: Frightened enough to lose sleep, and worried for his partner's job as well as his own.
S2.quote: Well, at least the cows will be looked after.
S2.fieldNote: This is where Yusuf's confidence goes. His instinct is collective: the union, the MP, the job centre, his mother. He doesn't look for an individual escape at all, and is clear-eyed that he wouldn't find one. The dark joke about the cows told more than any of his direct answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same end point, with a bit more warning. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really, but louder and earlier. With five years, the union's got time to fight for something real, like a law that says you can't sack farm workers for a robot without paying them a year's wages. I'd be telling everyone to join now, not when it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years scares me in a different way. I know myself, I'd keep telling myself next year I'll sort it out. I'd probably still be at Hollins in year four, hoping Martin's too old-fashioned to buy in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get Ines to sit me down and make a plan, because I won't do it on my own. Save harder, maybe a hundred and fifty a week, and get on the union's campaign group. I'd vote for whoever promised to make the robot companies pay into a fund for workers, and I'd go door to door for them if the branch asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a slower worry. Like a bill you know is coming in the post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still be hoping in year four. Is there anything that would push you to move earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Craig took over and bought a robot, that'd do it. Or if the union said, look, we've got a training deal, everyone sign up. I'd go if other people were going. I won't be the first one through the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Dennis, who does the tractor work part-time. He's sixty-three and he's never had a bank card that wasn't paper statements. If it's hard for me, I don't know what he'd do.

S3.say: I'd say it louder and earlier: with five years the union can fight for a law that makes farms pay a year's wages if a robot replaces a worker. I'd tell everyone to join now.
S3.think: I know I'd keep putting it off and still be at the farm in year four, hoping my boss is too old-fashioned to buy robots. The time scares me because I won't use it well.
S3.do: Asks his partner to help him make a plan and raises saving to about a hundred and fifty a week. Joins the union campaign group and votes and canvasses for a fund paid by robot companies.
S3.feel: A slower, steadier dread, like a bill he knows is in the post.
S3.quote: I'd go if other people were going. I won't be the first one through the door.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time doesn't make Yusuf calmer; he worries he'll waste it, which is unusually self-aware. What would move him is other people moving, through the union. He thought of an older colleague before himself when asked who he'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one, with the most warning. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for the country to get it right if it wants to. Shorter weeks, shared-out work, something like that. I'd say it at the union and probably get told I'm dreaming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years sounds so far away that I'd probably do nothing for the first five. I'd be thirty-seven when it arrives, which is young enough to start again but old enough that I'd have wasted my best years on a job that ended. That's the bit that stings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Hollins and keep saving. Maybe in a few years, if the union ran courses, I'd do something with my hands that's slower to go, like fencing or drystone walling, I don't know. Mostly I'd wait and see what the government does, and stay in the branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than scared. It's far enough off that I can stop thinking about it when I'm milking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd have wasted your best years. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I left the feed mill to come farming because I wanted something that couldn't be done by a machine in a shed. If it all goes in ten years, I'd have picked the wrong thing twice. My dad said I should have done plumbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you were cutting back and saving hard. Here you'd mostly wait. Which is closer to the real you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The waiting, if I'm honest. When it's close I panic and do things. When it's far off I just get on with the cows. Ines says I'm like that with the dentist too.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for the country to get it right, with shorter weeks and work shared out, if it wants to. People at the union might tell me I'm dreaming.
S4.think: Ten years feels so far off that I'd probably do nothing for the first five. I'd be thirty-seven, young enough to start again but sore at having spent my best years on a job that ended.
S4.do: Keeps working at the farm and keeps saving while staying active in his union branch. Thinks about a slower-to-automate hands-on course such as fencing in a few years, but mostly waits to see what the government does.
S4.feel: Uneasy rather than scared, with a sting of regret about his choice of work.
S4.quote: If it all goes in ten years, I'd have picked the wrong thing twice. My dad said I should have done plumbing.
S4.fieldNote: When the danger is far off, Yusuf goes back to his routine, and he admits it openly, comparing it to avoiding the dentist. The regret about leaving the feed mill for farming is the emotional centre here. He still trusts the union to carry him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. What would help is money coming in while I find my feet, paid by the people making the robots, and a union that's already sat down with the farmers. And someone to show me the new thing slowly, without making me feel thick.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. Everyone talks about jobs, but a robot doesn't notice a cow is off her feed because she's standing funny. Maybe it will one day. I'd just like someone to check before they find out the hard way.

headlineQuote: A robot doesn't notice a cow is off her feed because she's standing funny.
portrait: Yusuf Silva is a 27-year-old dairy hand on Hollins Farm who left a feed mill to work with animals and is still finding his feet three years in. He lives with his partner Ines, a care worker, in a damp rented cottage, with about four months of savings. He has never used an AI tool and is honest that he won't be quick to learn one, so he puts his trust in the union, the government and his family instead. Mild change leaves him calm, the steady version makes him think he'll be the first to go, and the two-year AGI picture keeps him awake. Given ten years, he admits he would mostly wait.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years is no time for someone slow with new things and only four months of savings.
whatWouldHelp: Income while he finds his feet, paid for by the companies making the robots, a union deal agreed with farmers in advance, and patient training that doesn't make him feel stupid.
